extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students in real analysis / advanced calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of core real-analysis/calculus theorems: local extrema, mean value theorems, L'Hospital, Taylor expansions, Riemann–Stieltjes integration, fundamental theorem of calculus, and uniform convergence of function sequences. Includes definitions, statements, proofs, examples and corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: local maximum / local minimum
rubrics_metrics.description: f has a local maximum at x0 if there exists an open ball B_delta(x0) so that f(x0) >= f(x) for any x in B_delta(x0). Similarly, f has a local minimum at x0 if f(x0) <= f(x) for any x in B_delta(x0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard metric-space definition used to identify interior extrema; prerequisite for applying Fermat's theorem about critical points. No scoring guidance beyond the condition that the inequality must hold in some neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: critical point
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:(a,b) -> R, a point x0 in [a,b] is called a critical point if f is not differentiable at x0 or f'(x0) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to characterize possible locations of interior extrema; note endpoints a,b are not interior points and are treated separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem: interior local extremum implies derivative zero (Fermat-type)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is defined over [a,b] and has a local maximum or local minimum at some x0 in (a,b), then x0 is a critical point of f (i.e., f'(x0)=0 if differentiable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits cases: if not differentiable at x0 done; otherwise compare one-sided difference quotients and use existence of derivative to deduce both one-sided derivatives are 0 hence derivative zero. Remark: conclusion cannot be made at endpoints a or b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolle's theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), then there exists some x0 in (a,b) such that f'(x0)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: if f constant done; otherwise continuous function on compact interval attains max/min; interior extremum exists and apply previous theorem. Typical hypotheses: continuity on closed interval and differentiability on open interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Mean Value Theorem (MVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there exists x0 in (a,b) so that f(b)-f(a)=f'(x0)(b-a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard proof: construct h(x)=f(x) - ((f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)) x which satisfies Rolle's theorem; MVT is central for many consequences (monotonicity, Taylor remainder proofs, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If f,g are continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there exists x0 in (a,b) such that (f(b)-f(a)) g'(x0) = (g(b)-g(a)) f'(x0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by applying Rolle's theorem to h(x) = (f(b)-f(a)) g(x) - (g(b)-g(a)) f(x). Used in proofs such as L'Hospital's Rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: sign of derivative implies monotonicity
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable on (a,b) then: (1) f' >= 0 implies f is increasing; (2) f' <= 0 implies f is decreasing; (3) f' = 0 implies f is constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply MVT to any subinterval [x1,x2] to find x0 with f(x2)-f(x1)=f'(x0)(x2-x1) and deduce inequalities. Useful for testing monotonicity from derivative sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: bounded derivative implies uniform continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:(a,b)->R is differentiable and f'(x) is bounded (|f'(x)| <= M for all x in (a,b)), then f is uniformly continuous on (a,b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: use MVT to show |f(x)-f(y)| <= M |x-y| which gives Lipschitz continuity and hence uniform continuity. Note: differentiability implies continuity, so differentiable on closed interval ensures uniform continuity by Heine-Cantor as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Intermediate Value Property for Derivatives (Darboux's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable on [a,b] and f'(a) < f'(b), then for each mu with f'(a) < mu < f'(b) there exists x0 in (a,b) so that f'(x0)=mu. Similarly if f'(a) > f'(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: consider g(x) = f(x) - mu * x, use that g' takes negative and positive values at endpoints so global minimum is interior and g'(x0)=0, hence f'(x0)=mu. Important consequence: derivatives have the intermediate value property even if not continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: possible discontinuities of derivative
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable on [a,b], then f'(x) can only have discontinuities of the second kind on [a,b] (i.e., it cannot have jump discontinuities / first-kind discontinuities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: a first-kind (jump) discontinuity would violate Darboux's theorem because some intermediate values would be omitted. The text outlines contradiction by selecting intervals where f' stays away from a missing value, contradicting intermediate value property.

rubrics_metrics.name: L'Hospital's Rule (one-sided version, Theorem 4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume f,g are differentiable on (a,b) with g(x) != 0. If either (1) lim_{x->a} f(x)=0 and lim_{x->a} g(x)=0; or (2) lim_{x->a} |g(x)|=+∞, and lim_{x->a} f'(x)/g'(x) = A in [-∞,+∞], assuming g'(x) != 0 on (a,b), then lim_{x->a} f(x)/g(x) = A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof provided for finite a and finite A using Cauchy's mean value theorem; other cases left as exercises. Examples illustrate both 0/0 and ∞/∞ types and show when rule fails (example included). Must check hypotheses: differentiability, g' nonzero, and existence of limit of derivatives' quotient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: Lagrange form of remainder for first-order Taylor (Lemma 5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ C^1([a,b]) and f'' exists on (a,b), then for each x in (a,b] there exists xi in (a,x) so that R2(x) = f''(xi)/2 * (x-a)^2 where R2 is the remainder after first-order (linear) approximation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via constructing auxiliary function h(t) and applying Rolle's theorem twice to obtain xi. This is the basis for higher-order remainder estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor's Theorem with remainder (Theorem 5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ C^n([a,b]) and f^{(n+1)} exists on (a,b), then for each x in (a,b] there exists xi in (a,x) such that R_{n+1}(x) = f^{(n+1)}(xi)/(n+1)! * (x-a)^{n+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof proceeds by repeated application of Rolle's theorem to an auxiliary function to locate xi. Provides Lagrange form of remainder allowing error estimates and checks whether f equals its Taylor series by taking limit of remainder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Taylor series
rubrics_metrics.description: For f ∈ C^∞((a,b)) and c in (a,b), the Taylor series about c is Σ_{n=0}^∞ f^{(n)}(c)/n! * (x-c)^n. f equals its Taylor series at x iff lim_{n->∞} R_{n+1}(x)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes that being C^∞ does not automatically imply function equals its Taylor series; remainder estimates from Taylor's theorem are used to verify equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem: termwise differentiation of power series (Theorem 5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ c_n x^n has radius of convergence R, then f(x)=Σ c_n x^n is differentiable on (-R,R) and f'(x)=Σ_{n=1}^∞ n c_n x^{n-1}; in fact f is C^∞ on (-R,R) with formula for k-th derivative and f^{(k)}(0)=k! c_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement notes that differentiation termwise preserves radius of convergence; uniform convergence / later uniformly convergence results justify interchange of operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem: Taylor expansion for power series (Theorem 5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ c_n x^n has radius R and a ∈ (-R,R), then f(x) can be written as a power series centered at a with coefficients f^{(k)}(a)/k!: f(x)=Σ_{k=0}^∞ f^{(k)}(a)/k! (x-a)^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof manipulates the original power series via binomial expansion and justifies term rearrangement by absolute convergence within radius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: partition, upper and lower sums (Riemann–Stieltjes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A partition P of [a,b] is a finite set a=x0 <= x1 <= ... <= xn=b. For bounded f and increasing α, on each subinterval define M_i = sup_{[x_{i-1},x_i]} f, m_i = inf_{[x_{i-1},x_i]} f and Δα_i = α(x_i)-α(x_{i-1}). Upper sum U(f,α;P)=Σ M_i Δα_i and lower sum L(f,α;P)=Σ m_i Δα_i. Upper integral is inf_P U, lower integral is sup_P L. f is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable w.r.t α if they coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the precise constructive definition of the Riemann–Stieltjes integral, with notation ∫_a^b f dα and set R(α)([a,b]) of integrable functions. Special case α(x)=x yields Riemann integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability criterion: upper-lower sums gap (Theorem 1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: f ∈ R(α)([a,b]) iff for each ε>0 there exists a partition P such that U(f,α;P) - L(f,α;P) < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence used repeatedly to show integrability: construct partitions making upper-lower difference arbitrarily small. Proof given by relating sup/inf of sums to integral via refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous functions are Riemann–Stieltjes integrable (Theorem 1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ C^0([a,b]) and α is increasing, then f ∈ R(α)([a,b]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses uniform continuity of f on compact [a,b] to make oscillation on small intervals small, bounding U - L by ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone integrability (Theorem 1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is monotonic and α is continuous on [a,b], then f ∈ R(α)([a,b]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses uniform continuity of α and telescoping sum estimates; special case of constant f trivial. Works because α continuous controls Δα_i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability with finitely many discontinuities (Theorem 1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is bounded on [a,b] with only finitely many discontinuities and α is continuous at those points, then f ∈ R(α)([a,b]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof partitions neighborhoods around discontinuities small in α-measure and applies integrability on closed subintervals where f is continuous; combines estimates to make U-L small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves integrability (Theorem 1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ R(α)([a,b]) with m <= f <= M and g ∈ C^0([m,M]), then g ∘ f ∈ R(α)([a,b]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses uniform continuity of g and partitions where f-range on subintervals is small to control oscillation of g∘f; splits partition into intervals with small f-oscillation and the rest whose α-measure is small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of Riemann–Stieltjes integral (Theorem 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collection of properties: linearity in f (sum and scalar multiple), linearity in α (additivity), monotonicity (if f1 <= f2 then integrals order), additivity over intervals, bound |∫ f dα| <= M(α(b)-α(a)) if |f|<=M, product integrability if f,g integrable, |f| integrable and ∫|f| >= |∫ f|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each property proved via upper/lower sum inequalities and partition refinements; equality statements and inequalities given with brief proofs or exercises. Useful as checklist of algebraic and order properties for manipulating integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation with Riemann integral when α' exists (Theorem 2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If α' exists and α' ∈ R([a,b]), and f is bounded, then f ∈ R(α)([a,b]) iff f α' ∈ R([a,b]). In that case ∫_a^b f dα = ∫_a^b f(x) α'(x) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses mean value theorem on each subinterval to write Δα_i = α'(t_i) Δ_i and compares upper/lower sums; handles error using integrability of α' and boundedness of f. This gives substitution formula when dα = α'(x) dx.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of variable for Riemann–Stieltjes (Theorem 2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ is strictly increasing and continuous mapping [A,B] to [a,b], β = α ∘ φ is increasing on [A,B], and g = f ∘ φ, then g ∈ R(β)([A,B]) and ∫_A^B g dβ = ∫_a^b f dα.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: partitions correspond under φ and upper/lower sums match; used to derive substitution formulas for integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of variable for Riemann integral (Theorem 2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ R([a,b]) and φ maps [A,B] to [a,b] strictly increasing with φ' ∈ R([A,B]), then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∫_A^B f(φ(y)) φ'(y) dy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from previous theorem and relation when dα = α'(x) dx. Standard substitution formula with φ' integrable hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus I (Theorem 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ R([a,b]) and F(x)=∫_a^x f(t) dt, then F ∈ C^0([a,b]). Furthermore, if f is continuous at x0 then F is differentiable at x0 with F'(x0)=f(x0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: boundedness of f gives Lipschitz-type estimate for continuity of F; differentiability at x0 obtained by averaging and using continuity of f at x0. Standard link between integral and antiderivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus II (Theorem 3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ R([a,b]) and there exists a differentiable F on [a,b] with F' = f, then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b)-F(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: partition and apply mean value theorem on each subinterval to represent telescoping sum by sample values f(t_i)Δ_i; compare with upper sums to bound difference by ε. Standard evaluation technique when antiderivative known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration by parts (Theorem 3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F,G are differentiable on [a,b] with F'=f ∈ R([a,b]) and G'=g ∈ R([a,b]), then ∫_a^b F(x) g(x) dx = F(b)G(b) - F(a)G(a) - ∫_a^b f(x) G(x) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: apply fundamental theorem to (F G)' = f G + F g and rearrange. Requires integrability of f and g and continuity of F,G.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: uniform convergence of sequence of functions (Definition 1.1, Ch.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence {f_n} on X uniformly converges to f if for every ε>0 there exists N (independent of x) so that |f_n(x)-f(x)| < ε for all x in X and n>=N. Notation f_n ⇉ f on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with pointwise convergence; uniform convergence allows interchange of limits and ensures preservation of properties like continuity. Examples illustrate failure of uniformity (x^n on [0,1]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence quantified by sup norm (Theorem 1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given pointwise limit f_n -> f, define ε_n = sup_{x∈X} |f_n(x)-f(x)|. Then f_n ⇉ f iff ε_n -> 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent characterization useful for proving/non-proving uniform convergence via supremum norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence (Theorem 1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence {f_n} uniformly converges on X iff it is uniformly Cauchy: for every ε>0 there exists N such that for all m,n>=N and all x in X, |f_m(x)-f_n(x)|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for showing existence of uniform limit without explicitly constructing it; proof uses completeness of R pointwise and then uniform estimate to upgrade to uniform convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass M-test (Theorem 1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If functions a_n(x) satisfy |a_n(x)| <= M_n for all x and Σ M_n converges, then Σ a_n(x) converges uniformly on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard test for uniform convergence of series of functions; applied to power series to show uniform convergence on compact subsets inside radius of convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence preserves continuity (Corollary 2.2 / Theorem 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n ⇉ f on X and each f_n is continuous, then f is continuous. More generally, limits and pointwise limits can be interchanged under uniform convergence hypotheses as in Theorem 2.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses triangle inequality and uniform control; also Theorem 2.1 gives a general interchange-of-limits result: lim_{n->∞} lim_{x->x0} f_n(x) = lim_{x->x0} lim_{n->∞} f_n(x) under uniform convergence on a set S accumulating at x0.
